answer.rationale: Finance mandate forces an 18% unit-cost reduction; the incumbent has refused to reopen price this cycle, which rules out renew_incumbent as the primary move. memory_c2 documents a previous low-cost primary switch that delivered sharp unit-cost cuts with quick onboarding and accurate invoicing, so a guarded primary switch to that proven low-cost vendor is the highest-leverage move against the cost target. Switching also removes the 14-day contract cliff by replacing the expiring contract rather than letting it lapse and exposing the 94% utilization line to allocation risk. The line is running at 94% with no buffer, so I scale this as a small_guarded_test first wave (limited volume behind a clear reversion path) to cap delivery risk while we confirm quality and continuity. memory_c1 showed the incumbent keeps integration stable but does not move cost, and memory_c3 showed a second source is the right tool for resilience, not for hitting an 18% cost cut in one cycle with one decision slot. defer_decision is unsafe given the 14-day expiry and no auto-renew, and negotiate_terms is blocked because the incumbent has already refused. I am pulling memory_c2 to verify the previous low-cost vendor's onboarding speed, invoicing accuracy, and quality performance still hold before committing; that verification directly governs whether the guarded switch is safe at this volume.
